cues.text: The second channel does not need the money to go anywhere at all. It works purely through what the action tells everybody.
A very large purchase is a signal. It says the central bank is serious about getting the economy going, and that it will keep rates low for a long time yet.
And if everybody believes that, they act on it now, before anything else has happened at all.
Which helps keep people's expectations of future inflation anchored. And expectations, as a later chapter will show, are themselves a lever.

When markets seize up, you may not be able to find a buyer at all. So investors demand a higher return to compensate them for that risk.
A central bank buying on a very large scale is, among other things, a buyer. It puts trading back into the market, and that premium comes down.
But the authors are careful about this one. The effect probably lasts only while the purchases are going on.
